meshelium.popup.opengl.title: Meshelium needs the Vulkan renderer
meshelium.popup.opengl.body: Meshelium is installed, but Minecraft is drawing with its OpenGL renderer, so Meshelium is staying off. Meshelium's faster terrain rendering only works on the Vulkan renderer. You can switch right here; the change takes effect the next time the game starts. You can also switch any time in Options > Video Settings > Graphics API.
meshelium.popup.opengl.body.sodium: Meshelium is installed alongside Sodium, but Minecraft is drawing with its OpenGL renderer. Sodium is drawing the terrain on its own and Meshelium's mesh-shader speed-up is staying off: Meshelium can draw Sodium's chunks with mesh shaders, but only on the Vulkan renderer. You can switch right here; the change takes effect the next time the game starts. You can also switch any time in Options > Video Settings > Graphics API.
meshelium.popup.opengl.body.sodium_no_ad: Meshelium is installed alongside Sodium, and Minecraft is drawing with its OpenGL renderer. Sodium is drawing the terrain on its own. On this game loader Meshelium cannot yet draw Sodium's chunks, so switching to Vulkan will not turn Meshelium's terrain rendering on while Sodium is installed; Meshelium still lets you set a render distance above 32. You can switch renderers here or any time in Options > Video Settings > Graphics API.
meshelium.popup.restart.title: Restart Minecraft to apply
meshelium.popup.restart.body: Done: the Vulkan renderer is now selected. Minecraft only switches renderers while starting up, so the change applies the next time you launch the game. Quitting from a world saves it first, exactly as the pause menu does.
meshelium.popup.no_mesh.title: Meshelium is staying off
meshelium.popup.no_mesh.body: The Vulkan renderer is running, but this computer's graphics card or driver doesn't offer the mesh shader feature Meshelium needs (VK_EXT_mesh_shader). Minecraft will keep rendering the normal way: everything works, just without Meshelium's speed-up. A newer graphics driver may add support on some cards.
meshelium.popup.no_mesh.body.sodium: The Vulkan renderer is running, but this computer's graphics card or driver doesn't offer the mesh shader feature Meshelium needs (VK_EXT_mesh_shader). Sodium keeps drawing the terrain on its own: everything works, just without Meshelium's speed-up. A newer graphics driver may add support on some cards.
meshelium.popup.vulkan_failed.title: Vulkan didn't start
meshelium.popup.vulkan_failed.body: The Vulkan renderer is selected in your settings, but Minecraft couldn't start it and fell back to the OpenGL renderer, so Meshelium is staying off. A graphics driver update may fix this. The renderer setting is in Options > Video Settings > Graphics API.
meshelium.popup.vulkan_failed.body.sodiu: The Vulkan renderer is selected in your settings, but Minecraft couldn't start it and fell back to OpenGL. Sodium is drawing the terrain on its own and Meshelium's mesh-shader speed-up is staying off. A graphics driver update may fix this. The renderer setting is in Options > Video Settings > Graphics API.
meshelium.options.tooltip.menu: Opens Meshelium's settings. With Sodium installed, Video Settings usually opens Sodium's screen instead of Minecraft's, so Meshelium's settings also live here.
meshelium.options.title: Meshelium Options
meshelium.options.fog_end.label: Fog Ends At: %s%% of view
meshelium.options.tooltip.fog: Minecraft's distance haze stops at a fixed 1024 blocks however far you can see, so past 64 chunks it covers most of the view. Off removes it and keeps the short fade at the very edge. Match View Distance moves it out with your render distance instead.
meshelium.options.tooltip.fog_end: How far out the haze finishes, as a share of how far you can see. 100%% ends it right at the horizon. Lower for a moodier, hazier look, higher for a clearer one.
meshelium.options.advanced.title: Meshelium Advanced
meshelium.options.advanced.locked: Meshelium is not running, so these settings will not do anything until it is. See the main Meshelium settings screen for why.
meshelium.options.advanced.locked.sodium: Sodium builds the chunks and Meshelium draws them. Only the settings that still do something are shown here. Settings that only change how Meshelium builds chunks are hidden, because Sodium does that job. They come back if you remove Sodium.

Sodium is building the chunks and Meshelium is not drawing them, so these settings do nothing for now - except the startup notice at the bottom, which works on every renderer. The main Meshelium screen says why. Settings that only change how Meshelium builds chunks are hidden, because Sodium does that job. They come back if you remove Sodium.
meshelium.options.plant_cull.label: Cull Tiny Plants Beyond: %s
meshelium.options.detail_cull.label: Cull Sub-Pixel Detail Beyond: %s
meshelium.options.smart_leaves.label: Smart Leaves Beyond: %s
meshelium.options.solid_leaves.label: Solid Leaves Beyond: %s
meshelium.options.farfield.title: Meshelium Far Terrain
meshelium.options.farfield.radius.label: LOD Distance: %s
meshelium.options.farfield.band.note: Surface Only is what keeps this cheap: about three quarters of the block faces in a chunk are underground, where nothing far away can see them. Everything saves caves too and takes roughly four times the disk space.
meshelium.options.tooltip.farfield: Terrain far past your render distance, drawn from places you have already been. Off by default. The page has its own settings, the folder it saves to, and a button to delete it all.
meshelium.options.tooltip.farfield.enabl: Keeps a small record of the terrain you travel through and draws it far beyond your render distance, so the horizon does not simply stop. It only shows places you have already been, and it fills in as you explore. Off is the default and costs nothing at all: no disk space, no memory, no background work.
meshelium.options.tooltip.farfield.radiu: How far out saved terrain is drawn, in chunks. This is the cheap distant terrain Meshelium builds from places you have already been, which is why it can reach so much further than your render distance. Very large numbers may stop short of the number shown: your graphics card has a fixed budget for terrain, and when it fills the horizon simply stops where it got to. Nothing goes missing and nothing breaks when that happens, the distant view is just smaller than you asked for.
meshelium.options.tooltip.farfield.band: Surface Only saves just the top of the world, about eight blocks down from the surface, and that is what makes saving terrain affordable at all: roughly three quarters of a chunk's block faces are underground where nothing far away can see them. Everything saves caves and mines as well, for about four times the disk space.
meshelium.options.tooltip.farfield.folde: Where the saved terrain lives on disk. One folder per world, inside your game folder.
meshelium.options.tooltip.farfield.size: How much disk space the saved terrain is using right now, counting every world. Checked in the background, so it can be a couple of seconds behind.
meshelium.options.farfield.status: Far terrain: %s sections drawn, %s chunks saved this session
meshelium.options.tooltip.farfield.statu: Sections drawn is how much distant terrain is on screen right now. Chunks saved counts what has been recorded since you started the game. If both are zero, nothing has been saved here yet: the far terrain only records places you travel through after you turn it on, so walk a few hundred blocks and look back.
meshelium.options.tooltip.farfield.clear: Deletes the saved terrain for every world. The distant view goes back to normal and fills in again as you travel. This cannot be undone.
meshelium.options.applies.new_cache: Changes what gets saved, so it cannot be added to terrain that is already saved. The ground still loaded around you is saved again within about a minute; anything further out keeps the detail it has until you travel back through it.
meshelium.options.applies.far_now: Applies right away. The distant terrain clears all at once and rebuilds outwards from you over the next few seconds. The ground around you is untouched the whole time.
meshelium.options.applies.far_now_saved: Applies right away: the distant terrain clears all at once and rebuilds outwards from you over the next few seconds, with the ground around you untouched. Real Light also has to be saved with the terrain, and that is slower. The ground you are still holding is saved again over about a minute, and the horizon shows the real light once you have travelled back through it.
meshelium.options.applies.saving_rate: Applies right away, and only to how fast terrain is saved in the background. Nothing you can already see changes: the horizon keeps drawing exactly what it is drawing, nothing is thrown away, and nothing is saved again. All that moves is how much of each frame the game is allowed to spend turning the ground you have loaded into the horizon you will have later.
meshelium.options.applies.superseded: Locked, because another setting on this page already decides this exactly. Nothing you could set here would change a single pixel, so it is held rather than left to look live. Your choice is remembered and comes back the moment the other setting lets go of it.
meshelium.options.max_rd.label: Distance Cap: %s
meshelium.options.occlusion_rd.label: Auto turns on at: %s chunks
meshelium.options.applies.rebuild: Applies now; chunks rebuild for a few seconds.
meshelium.options.applies.new_builds: Applies to terrain as it builds; the world catches up over a few seconds.
meshelium.options.applies.restart: Applies at the next game start.
meshelium.options.applies.sodium: Held while Sodium builds the terrain: this only changes how Meshelium builds and stores its own.
meshelium.options.sodium.version: Sodium %1$s, the version this build of Meshelium was made for.
meshelium.options.sodium.version_mismatc: Sodium %1$s is installed. This build of Meshelium was made for Sodium %2$s. A different Sodium may not work: if the terrain looks wrong, put Sodium %2$s back, or start the game with -Dmeshelium.sodium.adapter=false to let Sodium draw all the terrain itself.
meshelium.options.tooltip.sodium_gpu: Lets Meshelium work out what you can actually see, on the graphics card, instead of drawing everything Sodium hands it. Sodium's list gets much bigger whenever you move the camera, which is what used to make the frame rate dip while you looked around. Leave it on unless you are chasing a problem; Meshelium falls back to the plain list by itself if it ever needs to.
meshelium.options.applies.sodium_gpu_hel: Only with Sodium installed and Meshelium drawing its chunks.
meshelium.options.status.ready: Meshelium: READY, renders when a world opens
meshelium.options.status.reason.sodium: Sodium is installed and is drawing the terrain by itself. Meshelium can draw it instead, using mesh shaders on Sodium's chunks, but that needs the Vulkan backend on a GPU that supports them.
meshelium.options.status.reason.sodium_n: Sodium is installed and is drawing the terrain by itself; on this game loader Meshelium cannot yet draw it instead
meshelium.options.status.reason.sodium_d: Sodium is drawing the terrain by itself; Meshelium's draw of its chunks was switched off with -Dmeshelium.sodium.adapter=false
meshelium.options.status.reason.sodium_n: Sodium is drawing the terrain by itself; Meshelium's mesh-shader draw of its chunks has not drawn a frame in this session
meshelium.options.status.sodium_ready: Working with Sodium. Sodium builds the chunks, Meshelium draws them with mesh shaders.
meshelium.options.status.sodium_active: Working with Sodium - drawing %s chunk sections with mesh shaders.
meshelium.options.status.reason.error: a renderer error occurred; vanilla is drawing
meshelium.toast.popup.title: Meshelium is off
meshelium.toast.launch.title: Your launcher skipped a Java setting
meshelium.toast.launch.shadow: Minecraft wants -XX:StackShadowPages=%s and got %s. Without it the game can close without a word. Add it to this instance's Java arguments.
meshelium.toast.popup.opengl: Minecraft is drawing with OpenGL. The chat line has the details.
meshelium.toast.popup.vulkan_failed: Vulkan is selected but it didn't start. The chat line has the details.
meshelium.toast.popup.no_mesh: No mesh shader support on this graphics card. The chat line has the details.
meshelium.chat.popup.opengl: Meshelium is not running because Minecraft is drawing with OpenGL. Open Options, then Video Settings, then Meshelium Settings to switch to the Vulkan renderer, or type /meshelium.
meshelium.chat.popup.opengl.sodium: Meshelium is not running because Minecraft is drawing with OpenGL, so Sodium is drawing the terrain alone. Open Options, then Meshelium, to switch to the Vulkan renderer, or type /meshelium.
meshelium.chat.popup.opengl.sodium_no_ad: Minecraft is drawing with OpenGL and Sodium is drawing the terrain. On this game loader Meshelium cannot draw Sodium's chunks on any renderer, so switching renderers will not turn its terrain rendering on. Type /meshelium to see what Meshelium still does.
meshelium.chat.popup.vulkan_failed: Vulkan is selected but Minecraft couldn't start it and fell back to OpenGL, so Meshelium is not running. A graphics driver update may fix this. Type /meshelium for the details.
meshelium.chat.popup.vulkan_failed.sodiu: Vulkan is selected but Minecraft couldn't start it and fell back to OpenGL, so Sodium is drawing the terrain alone and Meshelium is not running. A graphics driver update may fix this. Type /meshelium for the details.
meshelium.chat.popup.no_mesh: The Vulkan renderer is running, but this graphics card or driver doesn't offer the mesh shader feature Meshelium needs. Minecraft keeps drawing the terrain the normal way. Type /meshelium for the details.
meshelium.chat.popup.no_mesh.sodium: The Vulkan renderer is running, but this graphics card or driver doesn't offer the mesh shader feature Meshelium needs. Sodium keeps drawing the terrain on its own. Type /meshelium for the details.
meshelium.chat.error.renderer: Meshelium hit a graphics error and handed the terrain back to Minecraft for the rest of this session. The game log has the details.
meshelium.chat.error.coverage: Meshelium could not fit all of this world's terrain on your graphics card, so Minecraft is drawing it instead. Rejoin the world to try again.
meshelium.chat.error.residency: Meshelium hit a problem preparing terrain and stopped drawing it. The game log has the details.
meshelium.chat.seam.demoted: Meshelium is putting Minecraft's own terrain back. Chunks will rebuild for a few seconds.
meshelium.chat.seam.freeing: Meshelium is freeing Minecraft's duplicate copy of the terrain. Chunks will rebuild for a few seconds.
meshelium.chat.swap: Reloading the terrain so the renderers can swap. Chunks will rebuild for a few seconds.
meshelium.options.status.reason.passive: GPU budget exceeded; passive for this world
terrain memory %s MiB reached its %s MiB ceiling; passive for this world
one section's %s MiB mesh exceeded the %s MiB staging ring; passive for this world
region budget exhausted (%s of %s ids); passive for this world
your graphics card refused another %s MiB of terrain memory (%s MiB budget); passive for this world
a section failed to encode; passive for this world
meshelium.options.status.memory_free: Terrain memory: %s MB (%s MB free on the card)
meshelium.options.tooltip.status: Chunk sections are the 16 by 16 by 16 blocks Minecraft draws the world in. While Meshelium is running this counts the ones on screen, so it changes as you look around.
meshelium.options.tooltip.max_rd: How far Minecraft's own render distance slider is allowed to go. This does not change your distance by itself, it just raises the limit so you can pick a bigger number in Video Settings.
meshelium.options.tooltip.max_rd_custom: Type an exact limit, up to 120. That is as high as Minecraft can send a render distance. Big numbers use a lot of memory.
meshelium.options.tooltip.terrain: The whole mod, on or off. Meshelium draws terrain with mesh shaders, a faster way for the graphics card to handle lots of blocks. Off hands terrain back to Minecraft.
meshelium.options.tooltip.suppress_vanil: Minecraft keeps a second copy of the terrain in graphics memory even though Meshelium is the one drawing it. Freeing it saves several gigabytes at long render distances and costs nothing. Choose Kept only if another mod needs Minecraft's own terrain buffers. Changing this reloads the terrain, so chunks rebuild for a few seconds.
meshelium.options.tooltip.arena_trim: Meshelium grows its terrain memory in large steps and normally keeps the spare room committed. With this on, after half a minute of no terrain activity it hands the unused part back to your graphics card, which can be several hundred megabytes at long render distances. Flying somewhere new simply takes the memory again. Turn it off only if another mod misbehaves when graphics memory shrinks.
meshelium.options.tooltip.greedy_meshing: Merges neighbouring block faces into single larger ones, so there is less geometry to draw. How much it saves depends on Smooth Lighting: with it off it removes about one face in six, with it on nearer one in twenty, because Minecraft shades each corner separately and two differently shaded faces usually cannot become one. Expect a few percent more frames, most of it at long render distances. The picture is identical either way.
meshelium.options.tooltip.plant_cull: Past this distance, small plants like grass and flowers are not drawn. They are smaller than a pixel long before this matters, so the view should look the same and draw a little faster. Off draws everything, everywhere.
meshelium.options.tooltip.detail_cull: Past this distance, anything that would end up smaller than one pixel on your screen is skipped. Off draws everything.
meshelium.options.tooltip.smart_leaves: Past this distance, new terrain drops the leaf faces hidden inside tree canopies, which in a forest is roughly a fifth of all geometry. Leaves keep their see-through look: only faces buried where you could never see them are dropped. Trees regain their full detail as you approach, and turning this down or off rebuilds the affected chunks over a few seconds. Off changes nothing.
meshelium.options.tooltip.solid_leaves: Past this distance, full see-through blocks like leaves are built fully solid, the way Fast graphics draws leaves everywhere. Thin details like flowers, vines and tall grass keep their normal look. This helps most in big forests, and it lets distant woods hide whatever is behind them instead of drawing it. Trees regain their see-through look as you approach, and turning this down or off rebuilds the affected chunks over a few seconds. Off changes nothing.
meshelium.options.tooltip.debug_stats: Writes a line about the renderer to your log every 5 seconds. Handy in a bug report. Does not change how the game looks or runs.
meshelium.options.tooltip.popup: Show the startup notice again if Meshelium cannot run, for example when Minecraft is using the OpenGL renderer.
meshelium.options.tooltip.enable_vulkan: Selects the Vulkan renderer in Minecraft's own settings. The switch happens at the next game start.
meshelium.options.gate.opengl: Meshelium is off: Minecraft is drawing with OpenGL. Switch to Vulkan and these settings come alive at the next game start.
meshelium.options.gate.no_mesh: Meshelium is off: this graphics card or driver has no mesh shader support (VK_EXT_mesh_shader).
meshelium.options.gate.no_mesh.sodium: Meshelium is off. This graphics card or driver does not have the mesh shader feature Meshelium needs, so Sodium is drawing the terrain by itself. Settings that only change how Meshelium builds chunks are hidden, because Sodium does that job. They come back if you remove Sodium.
meshelium.options.gate.unknown: Meshelium works out which renderer it is on a moment after the game finishes loading. This screen refreshes itself when it has.
meshelium.options.gate.sodium: Working with Sodium: settings that only change how Meshelium builds chunks are hidden, because Sodium does that job. They come back if you remove Sodium.
meshelium.options.gate.sodium_declined: Sodium is drawing the terrain by itself, because Meshelium was told to stay out of it this session. The Distance Cap above still works. Settings that only change how Meshelium builds chunks are hidden, because Sodium does that job. They come back if you remove Sodium.
meshelium.options.gate.sodium_opengl: Meshelium is off. Minecraft is drawing with OpenGL, so Sodium is drawing the terrain by itself. Switch to Vulkan and Meshelium takes over the drawing next time you start the game. Settings that only change how Meshelium builds chunks are hidden, because Sodium does that job. They come back if you remove Sodium.
meshelium.options.gate.sodium_no_adapter: Sodium is drawing the terrain by itself. On this game loader Meshelium cannot draw Sodium's chunks yet. The Distance Cap above still works. Settings that only change how Meshelium builds chunks are hidden, because Sodium does that job. They come back if you remove Sodium.
meshelium.options.gate.vulkan_failed: Vulkan is selected but Minecraft couldn't start it and fell back to OpenGL, so Meshelium is off. A graphics driver update may fix this.
meshelium.options.gate.vulkan_failed.sod: Meshelium is off. Vulkan is chosen in your settings but Minecraft could not start it and used OpenGL instead, so Sodium is drawing the terrain by itself. A newer graphics driver may fix this. Settings that only change how Meshelium builds chunks are hidden, because Sodium does that job. They come back if you remove Sodium.
meshelium.options.dev_override: Some rows are locked: a -D dev flag on the command line is overriding them for this session.
meshelium.options.tooltip.occlusion: Skips drawing terrain that is hidden behind other terrain. It helps on some systems and hurts on others, and mostly only pays off at longer render distances. Auto switches it on past the distance where it usually helps. Safe to try either way.
meshelium.options.tooltip.occlusion_rd: The render distance Auto switches it on at. Lower it if you play mostly on the ground or in caves, raise it if you fly a lot. On laptop or integrated graphics, try 32.
meshelium.options.tooltip.occlusion_rd_c: Type an exact distance. 2 keeps it always on, 120 keeps it off.
meshelium.options.tooltip.reset: Puts every Meshelium setting back to normal. Minecraft's own settings are left alone.
meshelium.options.tooltip.reset.sodium: Puts every Meshelium setting back to normal, including the chunk-builder settings this screen does not show while Sodium is installed. Minecraft's own settings are left alone.
meshelium.options.tooltip.advanced.sodiu: Settings that almost nobody needs to change: the detail cull, logging, and the startup notice.
meshelium.rd.clamped.title: Render distance limited to %s
meshelium.rd.clamped.off: Meshelium isn't drawing here, so the extended render distance was turned back down. The vanilla renderer above 32 chunks would run far too slowly.
meshelium.rd.clamped.passive: Meshelium went passive for this world (terrain didn't fit its GPU budget), so the render distance was restored for smooth play. It can be raised again in a fresh world.
meshelium.rd.restored.title: Render distance back to %s
meshelium.rd.restored.body: Meshelium is drawing again, so the distance it had to turn down while it was off has been put back.
meshelium.rd.rejoin.title: Rejoin to apply fully
meshelium.rd.rejoin.body: Render distance %s needs bigger GPU buffers than this world could grow to (sized %s chunks). Everything keeps working; rejoin the world to apply the full distance.
meshelium.rd.pressure.title: Render distance lowered to %s
meshelium.rd.pressure.body: Meshelium ran out of room on your graphics card for terrain this far out, so it pulled the distance in rather than let chunks go missing. It stays where it is now; raise it again in Video Settings whenever you like.
meshelium.options.applies.planned: Not used yet. Arrives in a later update.
meshelium.options.applies.retired: Retired, because Minecraft already does both of the things this used to do. Leaving it switchable would only let you undo them, so it is held rather than left to look live. Nothing you set here changes a pixel.
meshelium.options.farfield.preset.label: Preset: %s
meshelium.options.tooltip.farfield.prese: Sets everything on this page at once. No LOD turns distant terrain off entirely and loads real chunks out to 32. Highest Detail keeps render distance 32 and draws saved terrain out to 64 chunks. Balanced halves the render distance to 16 and keeps all 64 chunks of saved terrain, which is the best trade on most machines because real chunks are the expensive half. Performant uses 12 and 48, Ultra Performant uses 8 and 32. Change any single setting afterwards and this reads Custom, with your values left exactly as you set them.
meshelium.options.tooltip.farfield.rende: Minecraft's own render distance, the same setting as in Video Settings. These are real chunks with everything in them, so this is the expensive number: turning it down and letting saved terrain fill the view is what makes a big horizon affordable. Takes effect when you let go of the slider.
meshelium.options.farfield.layers.note: Each layer is a ring of distant terrain at its own distance, with its own list of savings you can turn on. Layer 1 is the only one in use today, and it is set up to look like ordinary terrain.
meshelium.options.farfield.planned.layer: Layer %s is not in use yet. The settings below are saved now and will be used the moment this layer arrives in a later update. Nothing here changes your game today.
meshelium.options.tooltip.farfield.l1: The first ring of distant terrain, starting where your render distance ends. It is meant to look like ordinary terrain, so nothing on it is simplified unless you say so here.
meshelium.options.tooltip.farfield.l2: A second ring beyond Layer 1, meant to be cheap enough to reach much further. Not in use yet; the page shows what it will offer.
meshelium.options.tooltip.farfield.l3: The furthest ring, for the cheapest possible horizon. Not in use yet; the page shows what it will offer.
meshelium.options.farfield.l1.title: Far Terrain Layer 1
meshelium.options.farfield.l2.title: Far Terrain Layer 2
meshelium.options.farfield.l3.title: Far Terrain Layer 3
meshelium.options.farfield.l1.about: Layer 1 begins where your render distance ends. Its job is to look like ordinary terrain: only the surface you could actually see is drawn, and everything else about it stays at full quality unless you change it here.
meshelium.options.farfield.l2.about: Layer 2 sits beyond Layer 1. It exists to be cheap, so it can cover far more ground for the same memory once you tell it what it is allowed to give up.
meshelium.options.farfield.l3.about: Layer 3 is the furthest ring, for the cheapest possible horizon on the very biggest views.
meshelium.options.tooltip.farfield.layer: Whether this ring of distant terrain is drawn at all. Turning it off releases everything it was drawing over the next few seconds, and turning it back on fills it in again the same way.

How far this ring reaches, in chunks, measured from you. Very large numbers may stop short of the number shown: your graphics card has a fixed budget for terrain, and when it fills the horizon simply stops where it got to.

How much frame rate the game may spend saving distant terrain. The horizon is drawn from ground you have already loaded, so it can only exist once that ground has been written down, and writing it down costs about a millisecond a chunk. Fast, the default, uses the spare time in a frame while you travel and, while you are standing still with terrain still waiting, up to half of it: on a machine running 120 frames a second that shows up as roughly 84 until the waiting terrain is done, and it goes straight back to 120 the moment it is. Balanced keeps the travelling half and drops the standing-still half, so your frame rate never moves while you are not moving and a big view takes several times longer to finish. Gentle spends half the standard sliver of each frame and nothing more, whatever the machine has spare - the slowest setting, and the only one that is slower than Balanced even on a fast machine; a very large view may then take longer to save than you are willing to stand around for. None of the three can lose terrain: ground that unloads before it is written down is held and written out by a background helper that does not use frame time at all, whatever this dial says. None of the three changes how anything looks, none of them changes what is saved, and none of them can cause a stutter: every setting here is a ceiling on time already measured out, and the longest single pause the saver can produce is the same on all three.
Saving: distant terrain is turned off
meshelium.options.farfield.layer.saving_: Saved %s chunks (%s partial), %s still waiting (%s out of date)
meshelium.options.tooltip.farfield.layer: How much of the ground you have seen this session has been written down as distant terrain - everything you have loaded since joining, not just what is around you right now. Waiting counts the chunks you are holding that still need to be written; when it reaches zero and the line below shows nothing leaving, this line turns green and everything you have seen is saved - that is the moment it is safe to turn your render distance down. Partial means a chunk was written down while one of its neighbours was missing, so its cliffs can be cut off at the chunk edge; those fix themselves the next time you load that ground with its neighbours. Out of date means you have changed blocks there since it was last written and it is queued to be written again. The numbers refresh about once a second.
meshelium.options.farfield.layer.saving_: Being saved in the background: %s  |  behind: %s  |  lost: %s
meshelium.options.tooltip.farfield.layer: When ground unloads before it has been written down, the game keeps hold of it and a background helper writes it out over the next seconds - it does not race your frame rate and it does not depend on the dial above. There is no limit on how much can be held this way; even dropping a huge render distance hands everything over. Behind counts chunks whose latest changes did not reach disk - they catch up by themselves the next time you visit that ground. Lost counts the ones that are gone for good, which can only happen if the game runs out of memory while holding them or the world closes before the last few seconds of writing finish. Both numbers staying at zero is normal; if either climbs on an ordinary session, that is a bug worth reporting, not something a setting can fix.

How finely this ring is rebuilt. Full keeps every block. Half merges each group of two by two by two blocks into one, which costs roughly a quarter of the memory and lets the ring reach much further. Quarter goes one step further again. Distant hills keep their shape either way; small details are what go.

Saves and draws plants that stand in water: kelp, seagrass, coral and anything else underwater. Without this they are missing entirely, because a block surrounded by water has no face against open air and nothing tells the saver it is there. Cost: nothing at all in a plain ocean, because it only ever applies to a block that would be drawn as a plant. In a thick kelp forest it can more than double what that chunk costs on disk, and each kelp block draws four crossed pieces, so a kelp chunk carries far more shapes than the water around it.

This used to keep small see-through blocks like torches, bars, posts and lanterns from thinning out in the distance. It turns out Minecraft already does both halves of that itself, and doing them a second time was what made distant kelp stand above the water as a green smear and leaf piles and flower beds draw as black patches. A torch was never at risk: its texture is solid all the way to the edges, so the game draws it as a solid block and none of this ever applied to it. Nothing is lost by holding this row.

How grass, leaves and water colours change across the world. Per Chunk saves one colour for each kind of block in each chunk, so a boundary between two biomes jumps at the chunk edge and two chunks side by side never blend, which is what makes distant oceans look like two flat colours. Per Block saves the colour Minecraft itself would draw for every single block, so a biome edge fades over exactly the same distance it does up close and neighbouring chunks line up perfectly. Cost: nothing worth measuring inside a single biome, because a chunk of one colour is still stored as one colour. Where two biomes meet, Per Block adds roughly 700 bytes per kind of coloured block in that chunk, on a chunk that costs about a kilobyte.

How distant terrain is lit. Real Light, the default, uses the world's actual light: a cave mouth is dark inside, trees cast shade on the ground under them, and a torch lights the blocks around it. The whole horizon follows day and night and your own Brightness slider exactly like the ground you are standing on, because both read the same lighting from the game. Glowing Blocks drops the saved light and keeps only each block's own glow, so distant torches, lanterns, glowstone and lava still read as lit but a cave looks like a hillside. Flat Daylight lights everything as if it were in full sun. Cost: Flat and Glowing are free. Real Light saves one extra byte for every block it saves, about a quarter more raw data and far less than that on disk, because most of the surface is plain daylight and a chunk that is all daylight saves no light at all. It only applies to terrain saved after you turn it on. Terrain already on the horizon keeps what it was saved with, because the real light is simply not in that file and no amount of redrawing can invent it, so a change here shows up as you travel back through the world rather than the moment you click. Smooth Lighting is the row that changes the horizon you can already see. One thing it does not do: distant terrain stores one light value per block, taken looking out of its most visible side, so a block tucked under a one block lip is lit by the open air beside it rather than by the lip.

How strong the shading above is. Slide it up for a heavier, more contrasty horizon and down for a flatter one, and set it to Off to turn the shading off entirely. On Full, 100 percent is exactly what the game draws up close, which is why it is the default: anything less would leave a visible step in shading where the distant terrain meets the ground around you. On Edges Only, 100 percent takes half the brightness off a corner where two shaded edges meet. Cost: none by itself. It only scales the shading the row above is already doing.

Draws distant water the way Minecraft draws the water at your feet. Under water, light loses one step for every block it passes through, so a sea bed three blocks down is half as bright, ten blocks down is barely there, and fifteen blocks down is black. That is what makes a real ocean read as one dark blue mass instead of a bright sea bed showing through a thin sheet, and it is Minecraft's own rule, not an effect. Stock Minecraft applies that rule to every distant chunk. Where the chunk was saved with its real light, the saved light already says exactly this and nothing is added; where it was not - terrain saved before you turned Real Light on, and terrain saved the moment a chunk arrived, before the game had finished working its light out - the same rule is worked out from the shape of the water instead, so both kinds of chunk draw the same ocean. As Saved uses only the light that was saved, which leaves those chunks bright and can put a pale ocean right next to a dark one. Either way, shallow water still shows its sand and gravel exactly as it does up close, and the shoreline matches the chunks around you because both use the same numbers. Cost: none. No extra memory, no extra shapes, no extra saved data, and it is one of the settings here that also fixes terrain you have already saved. Changing it reloads the distant terrain, and if every chunk out there already has its real light saved that reload comes back looking identical.

Vanilla's smooth lighting, at distance: the subtle darkening in the corners and along the edges where blocks meet, so hills, cliffs, ledges, tree trunks and cave mouths have shape instead of reading as one flat sheet of colour. Full is the real thing, worked out per corner the same way the ground around you is, so the darkening is one block wide and the horizon matches the near terrain where the two meet. Edges Only is the cheaper older version: it shades whole edges of the merged shapes the distant terrain is built from, which is free but spreads the shading much wider than one block. Off leaves every face one flat colour. All of it is worked out from the shape of the terrain rather than saved with it, which is why it also fixes every chunk you have already saved, and it never darkens a face unless a real block is standing against it, so an open plain stays exactly as bright as it was. Cost: Off and Edges Only are free. Full costs nothing on flat ground, where nothing is shaded and the terrain still draws as few large shapes, and up to about a sixth more shapes on broken ground like mountains and cliffs. One thing it cannot do: a block standing on the far side of a chunk line is invisible to it, so a line of shadow can stop one block short there. It stops short on both sides equally and it never draws shading that is not there, so it cannot draw a grid across the horizon.

Some blocks are drawn a different way round in every place they stand. Grass, dirt, sand, podzol, mycelium, netherrack, coarse dirt paths and the concrete powders each pick one of four turns of their top texture from where the block is, and stone, bedrock and sculk pick between two patterns, so a field or a cliff looks like ground rather than like one tile stamped over and over. On, distant terrain picks the same way round the game picks up close, so a grass plain matches the ground at your feet instead of showing one repeated pattern out to the horizon. Off, every one of those blocks is drawn the same way round out there. Cost: this is the one setting on this page that costs something on FLAT ground. Because neighbouring blocks are now turned different ways, the distant terrain cannot join them into one large shape any more, so a flat grass field or desert costs roughly twice as many shapes as it did. Hills, stone, forests, snow and water are unaffected. Nothing extra is saved to disk, and it also fixes terrain you have already saved.

Builds see-through blocks like leaves fully solid on this ring, the way Fast graphics draws leaves. Distant woods then hide whatever is behind them instead of drawing it, which is usually a large saving in a forest. Plants, ground cover and small parts like fence posts keep their see-through look. Cost: none, and it can help; the trade is that distant forests lose their gaps.
Draws large bodies of water on this ring as one flat sheet at the surface instead of following every block. Oceans are a big share of a saved world and nearly all of it sits at a single height.

How much block detail this ring keeps. Each step blurs the textures further, and the last step replaces every block face with a single flat colour. This far out the difference is hard to see, and the graphics card does much less work.

Shades this ring in blocks of two by two pixels instead of one pixel at a time. At this distance it is the kind of change you only notice if you go looking for it, and on a big screen it can be a large saving.

Builds this ring from a single height per column of blocks rather than from saved blocks. It is by far the cheapest way to draw a horizon and by far the least detailed: hills and coastlines, and nothing else.
meshelium.options.farfield.layer.band_no: What gets saved to disk is one setting shared by every layer, because every layer draws from the same saved terrain. It is called Saved Detail and it lives on the Far Terrain page.
